Browser origin of window.outerWidth/outerHeight/screenX/screenY. THE deviceMemory PATTERN, REPEATED. On navigation requests the browser computes the DPR header itself: GetDeviceScaleFactor() at :142 reads display::Screen::Get()->GetPrimaryDisplay().device_scale_factor() directly from the browser's own display list, multiplied by GetZoomFactor() at :153 which reads HostZoomMap. It never consults the renderer. A renderer-only patch to LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio therefore makes Sec-CH-DPR on the navigation contradict window.devicePixelRatio in the document it loads. Two further stock divergences worth knowing: it uses the PRIMARY display, not the display the window is on, and it uses the host zoom map's level rather than the frame's composed layout zoom.

DEVICE PIXEL RATIO IS NOT A PASSTHROUGH. `ratio = page_->InspectorDeviceScaleFactorOverride(); ratio *= LayoutZoomFactor();`. LayoutZoomFactor is composed in WebFrameWidgetImpl::SetZoomInternal (web_frame_widget_impl.cc:2515-2518) as device_scale_factor * ZoomLevelToZoomFactor(zoom_level) * css_zoom_factor, where device_scale_factor is WebViewImpl::ZoomFactorForViewportLayout() (web_view_impl.h:182), itself set from ScreenInfo::device_scale_factor in WebFrameWidgetImpl::DidUpdateSurfaceAndScreen (:5419). So page zoom IS folded in: at 110% zoom on a 2x display window.devicePixelRatio is 2.2, not 2. A patch that pins this function to a constant destroys the zoom relationship and makes every zoom level report the same ratio, which no real browser does. Patch ScreenInfo::device_scale_factor upstream instead and let the multiplication stand. This is the only place the product is formed, and window.devicePixelRatio, the CSS `resolution` / `-webkit-device-pixel-ratio` features and the renderer's own DPR client hint all read it.

Pure forwarder to LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio(). Patching here would leave the CSS `resolution` media feature and the DPR client hint reporting the host's real ratio — an in-page contradiction detectable with one matchMedia call.
`return frame->DevicePixelRatio();` — identical source to window.devicePixelRatio.

It is a constant and must stay one.

Derives the gamut bucket from ScreenInfo::display_color_spaces.GetScreenInfoColorSpace(). The value therefore follows from the display colour space the browser installed; it is derived, not stored, so it is set by choosing a colour space, not by writing a bucket.

`GetScreenInfo(*frame).display_color_spaces.SupportsHDR()`. Same input as the 30-bit colour depth, so HDR is one fact with three faces.

The CSS `orientation` feature is VIEWPORT orientation, not display orientation: it compares media_values.Width() against Height() (:472-479) and treats a square viewport as portrait. It has no connection to screen.orientation.type, and a tall narrow window on a landscape monitor legitimately reports portrait in CSS and landscape-primary on screen.orientation. Any coherence rule forcing them equal would be wrong.

Both return RootWindowRect origin in virtual-screen coordinates, so on a multi-monitor host they leak the window's position across the whole desktop — including negative coordinates for a monitor left of or above the primary, which contradicts a single-display profile immediately.

innerHeight :1766, innerWidth :1775. Both are AdjustForAbsoluteZoom::AdjustInt(GetViewportSize(), LocalFrame::LayoutZoomFactor()) — the LayoutFrameView size in CSS pixels. The view size originates in the browser as VisualProperties::new_size; the CSS-pixel conversion happens here. Because the divisor is LayoutZoomFactor (DSF x zoom x css zoom), inner size and devicePixelRatio move together and a patch to one without the other breaks their product.

width :139, height :161, scale :183, offsetLeft :63, offsetTop :74. For the outermost main frame these forward to Page::GetVisualViewport(); for subframes they compute from the layout viewport's VisibleContentRect excluding scrollbars, divided by LayoutZoomFactor. Nothing here reads ScreenInfo.

Width :494 and Height :501 return VisibleWidthCSSPx()/VisibleHeightCSSPx() (:524, :533), built from VisibleRect (:439) which takes size_ (set by SetSize at :395 from the widget size), optionally excludes scrollbars, adds browser_controls_adjustment_ and divides by the pinch scale (:444-450). getClientRects :3351, GetClientRectsNoAdjustment :3365, GetBoundingClientRectNoLifecycleUpdateNoAdjustment :3384, GetBoundingClientRect :3411, GetBoundingClientRectForBinding :3417. No arithmetic of its own — the numbers are already fixed by the time this function sees them, which is exactly why a patch here would be a fabrication rather than a value.

Where rect numbers actually come from: the laid-out geometry, mapped to absolute coordinates. QuadsInAncestor is at :2474 and dispatches to the virtual QuadsInAncestorInternal (:3622), overridden per layout-object class. The storage is LayoutUnit, a fixed-point type holding multiples of 1/64 px (third_party/blink/renderer/platform/geometry/layout_unit.h:67, kFixedPointDenominator = 1 << kFractionalBits at :91). That constant is the whole explanation of the competitor artifact recorded in coh.layout-integer-positions: -10000.015625 is -10000 - 1/64 and -0.03125 is -2/64, i.e. a +-1 and +-2 perturbation of the raw LayoutUnit storage. Noise injected anywhere in this path is quantised to 1/64 px and is therefore identifiable as tampering rather than as a different device. The correct treatment is to leave this path untouched and make its inputs — fonts, zoom, DSF — correct.

The last transform applied to a client rect and the obvious place to inject noise — which is why it is named here explicitly as a place NOT to patch.

Every one of these matches the T0 capture exactly. Each other backend has its own equivalent (RendererVk, Renderer11, RendererGL), which is why the dump changes wholesale when the backend changes.

The third gate is where the ANGLE backend enters the extension list, and the fourth is where the GPU blocklist does.

Splits GpuFeatureInfo::disabled_webgl_extensions on spaces into disabled_extensions_ at :1381-1389. This is the concrete, page-observable consequence of a GPU blocklist decision: the blocklist is keyed on GPUInfo, and the extension list a page reads is filtered by it. gl_context->SetDisabledGLExtensions(disabled_extensions) at :33. The hop from a blocklist decision to a GL extension string the page can enumerate.

The single place where GPUInfo becomes configuration. Every one of the 142 workaround names in gpu/config/gpu_workaround_list.txt is also a command-line switch of the same name (kFeatureList is built from the same GPU_OP macro list at :22-28, and build_workaround_header.py:46 shows the name is the txt line verbatim). The switch lives on the GPU process command line and is not readable from a renderer, so using it adds no observable of its own.

Validates the enums then forwards ContextGL()->GetShaderPrecisionFormat at :4512 and wraps the result. No clamping, no substitution: the twelve triples a page can read come straight from the ANGLE backend's caps.

Only antialias carries device information, and it is decided in DrawingBuffer::Initialize.

Computed once into a function-local static, so it is fixed for the life of the renderer process - which is what makes it a profile setting rather than per-call behaviour.

Validates the destination view and format, calls ClearIfComposited, then reads the drawing buffer through the command buffer into the caller's ArrayBufferView. The WebGL2 entry points at webgl2_rendering_context_base.cc:833, :853 and :874 funnel into the same helper. There is no value stored here to overwrite - the bytes are whatever the GPU actually rendered, which is why this surface is escalated rather than assigned a spoof verdict.

Takes a StaticBitmapImage snapshot (:469) and readPixels into the ImageData buffer (:505-511). Two behaviours matter for determinism: when willReadFrequently is undefined, read_count_ is incremented and acceleration is disabled once it reaches kFallbackToCPUAfterReadbacks = 2 (base_rendering_context_2d.h:78, check at :461-466), so the first readback of a canvas can come from GPU raster and later ones from CPU raster; and a console warning is emitted on the second readback (:441-455), which is itself a weak observable.

Snapshot -> ImageDataBuffer -> ImageDataBuffer::ToDataURL. Returns the literal "data:," when the canvas is not paintable (:1282). The public entry at :1327 throws on a tainted canvas before reaching here. toBlob at :1351 takes the same encoding path.

Given identical pixels the encoded byte stream is a pure function of build constants: PNG through SkPngRustEncoder at CompressionLevel::kLow (:61), JPEG at default quality 92 (ComputeJpegQuality :109-114) with AlphaOption::kBlendOnBlack and Downsample::k444 only at quality 100 (:49-55), WebP at default quality 80 and lossless-at-75 when quality is exactly 1.0 (ComputeWebpOptions :116-131). No device input, no host input. Note the PNG encoder is the Rust one at this revision, so PNG bytes are Chromium-version-specific.

Decides whether canvas 2D is rastered on the GPU or the CPU, which is the largest single input to the rendered bytes after the backend itself. Gates: non-2D contexts never accelerate (:1476); RuntimeEnabledFeatures::Accelerated2dCanvasEnabled (:1480), set from --disable-accelerated-2d-canvas via web_contents_impl.cc:3816-3817; and the small-canvas cutoff kMinimumAccelerated2dCanvasSize = 128*129 (:168) at :1485-1496, which is guarded by AcceleratedSmallCanvasesEnabled. That feature is status "stable" (runtime_enabled_features.json5:229-230) and is only ever cleared on Android, so on desktop the cutoff does not apply and a typical small fingerprinting canvas IS GPU-rastered. SetPreferred2DRasterMode is chosen at :1562-1564 and downgraded to kPreferCPU when willReadFrequently is true.

Independent of HTMLCanvasElement::ShouldAccelerate: it asks Accelerated2DCanvasFeatureEnabled against SharedGpuContext::ContextProviderWrapper() and has no small-canvas cutoff and no willReadFrequently input. So an OffscreenCanvas in a worker and an HTMLCanvasElement on the main thread can be rastered by different backends for the same drawing operations.
The OffscreenCanvas readback path, alongside transferToImageBitmap at :296. Uses the same ImageEncoder constants as toDataURL.

ToCanvasRenderingContext2DSettings(CreationAttributes()) - a verbatim echo of what the author asked for, plus IDL defaults. Unlike the WebGL equivalent nothing is corrected against reality, so no device information reaches the page here.

Rejects non-finite coordinates and non-invertible transforms, inverse-maps the point through the CTM, then calls Path::Contains, i.e. SkPath::contains. Pure CPU floating-point path arithmetic - no rasterisation, no font, no GPU. isPointInStroke at :1881 is the stroke-geometry sibling and takes stroke width and join style into account but is likewise device-independent.

Where canvas text rasterisation is configured on macOS: SkFont::Edging is kSubpixelAntiAlias, kAntiAlias or kAlias depending on should_antialias and should_smooth_fonts (:244-250); embedded bitmaps are always off (:252); embolden and skew implement synthetic bold/italic (:255-256); setSubpixel and setLinearMetrics follow should_subpixel_position (:257-261); hinting is forced to kNone for -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased and text-rendering:geometricPrecision (:265-270). These flags plus the font file itself determine the glyph coverage bytes a canvas text fingerprint reads. Platform-specific: the Linux/Windows equivalents take their values from RendererPreferences instead.

Guarded by !IS_MAC in its entirety (:3645) — macOS takes none of this, which is why font_platform_data_mac.mm hard-codes its rasterisation flags instead. UPDATED ROW — line and body re-verified at 152.0.7977.82 (the GPU shard's :95-168 citation was exact); surfaces extended from canvas.measure-text alone to include the two fonts-text rows it also emits, now that the subsystem exists. width from MeasureRuns (:109-111); actualBoundingBoxLeft/Right from glyph bounds and the text-align delta (:128-129); fontBoundingBoxAscent/Descent from FontMetrics::FloatAscent/FloatDescent with ApplyBaselineTable(true) (:133-139); actualBoundingBox ascent/descent from glyph bounds (:140-141); em heights from NormalizedTypoAscentAndDescent (:144-147); alphabetic, hanging and ideographic baselines from the font's baseline table with arithmetic fallbacks (:151-168). This is a source of truth in the strongest sense: there is no other place a width could be substituted without contradicting the font file itself.

The hb_font_funcs callback HarfBuzz calls for every glyph. Where a font's raw ascent and descent become the integers a page can read. Default branch at :117-118 is SkScalarRoundToScalar on both. Two adjustments run ONLY under IS_LINUX||IS_CHROMEOS||IS_ANDROID||IS_FUCHSIA: VDMX bytecode-hinted metrics replace Skia's outright (:72-99, gated on hinting being full or normal, with a comment stating that CoreText and DirectWrite never bytecode-hint), and a descent-borrow that moves one unit from ascent to descent when subpixel positioning is on (:121-130). Same font file, same size, different integers depending on which OS the BINARY was built for — a divergence no profile field can carry, and the reason coh.font-metrics-platform-rounding is proposed. The comment at :101-104 says the code is designed to match Win32 metrics exactly except for these adjustments.

Calls font_.getMetrics then AscentDescentWithHacks (:126-133) and stores the results, then derives cap height (:137), underline position and thickness (:139-143), x-height with a hard-coded 0.56*ascent guess when the font supplies none (:163), line spacing as lroundf(ascent)+lroundf(descent)+lineGap (:175), and max char width as 2*ascent when the font supplies none (:188). The macOS answer to 'no font in the cascade has this glyph'. Emoji-presentation requests short-circuit to the literal kColorEmojiFontMac = "Apple Color Emoji" (:287, :318-323) before CoreText is consulted at all. Otherwise it optionally consults a per-character cache — gated on the codepoint being Ideographic=Yes and on RuntimeEnabledFeatures::MacCharacterFallbackCacheEnabled (:337-341), with a long comment (:326-336) explaining that caching fallback introduces CONTEXT SENSITIVITY, i.e. the same character can resolve differently depending on what was measured before it — worth knowing before treating any fallback measurement as stateless — and then hands the decision to GetAlternateFontPlatformData.

GetSubstituteFont (:127) calls CTFontCreateForString (:147, :149) and, for monochrome emoji requests, again against a mono emoji font (:180). GetAlternateFontPlatformData (:199) then reconciles weight and symbolic traits between the requested font and CoreText's substitute. Chromium expresses no fallback POLICY on macOS: the chain is whatever CoreText says it is for the installed set, which is exactly why the fallback cannot be reproduced on a host with a different font installation.

Hard-coded: font_family_names::kTimes with AlternateFontName::kAllowAlternate, and if that fails font_family_names::kLucidaGrande, whose comment says it is 'guaranteed to be there, according to Nathan Taylor'. Two macOS family names baked into the binary and reachable from JavaScript by requesting a cascade of families that do not exist. A profile that removes Times AND Lucida Grande from the claimed set contradicts this code path, so the profile's font list is not freely choosable — it has to keep the families the binary assumes.

The Linux counterpart, and structurally different from the macOS one. Emoji requests are rewritten to U+1F46A FAMILY before lookup (:71-77, with a FIXME admitting this is a hack); bold or italic requests first retry at standard style (:79-87); then GetFontForCharacter, and the returned FallbackFontData supplies a filepath, fontconfig interface id and ttc index (:100-103) rather than a family name. The font is then loaded BY PATH, so on Linux the identity of a fallback font is a file on disk, not a name.

Two branches: WebSandboxSupport::GetFallbackFontForCharacter when sandbox support exists — which it does in any real renderer — and gfx::GetFallbackFontForChar in-process otherwise (:56-63). The in-process branch is effectively test-only, so the observable behaviour of a shipped Chrome always takes the cross-process path.

Renderer-side stub over a mojo call. Keeps a per-codepoint memo under a lock (:41-48, :67-69) so a given character is asked about once per renderer, then calls font_loader_->FallbackFontForCharacter and copies family name, fontconfig interface id, filepath, ttc index and the bold/italic flags out of the reply (:55-66). No font data lives in the renderer. Confirms the general finding: on Linux the font list and the fallback decision are both gathered outside the sandbox.

The Linux source of truth for both 'is family X installed' and 'what covers codepoint C' (MatchFontWithFallback at :255, MatchFontByPostscriptNameOrFullFontName at :235 for local()). Process matters and is easy to get wrong: despite living under components/services, on Linux it is NOT a separate utility process — content/browser/font_service.cc:24-37 binds a function-local NoDestructor FontServiceApp onto a MayBlock ThreadPool sequence inside the BROWSER process. So the Linux equivalent of font_matcher_mac.mm runs in a different process than its macOS counterpart, and a fork that patches only the Blink font cache is correct on macOS and wrong on Linux.

The important finding is what this function does NOT do. For each family in the resolved list it `continue`s when the family is generic or when FontSelector::IsPlatformFamilyMatchAvailable is true (:257-260); otherwise it looks the name up in the FontFaceCache (:262-263) and only returns false when a CSSSegmentedFontFace EXISTS and fails CheckFont (:264-266). An uninstalled family with no @font-face rule produces a null face and falls through to `return true` at :269. document.fonts.check therefore reports on web fonts, not installed fonts, and the T0 capture shows it returning true for Segoe UI, Roboto and Noto Color Emoji on a host where the width probe finds none of them. Patching it to report the font set would CREATE a divergence from stock Chrome rather than remove one.

size() (:148) is CSSConnectedFontFaceList().size() + non_css_connected_faces_.size(), i.e. only @font-face rules and FontFace objects the page itself created — zero on a document with none, which is what T0 shows. status() (:56) is a ternary on is_loading_ returning 'loading' or 'loaded'. Neither carries host information; both are recorded so the row can be closed rather than left ambiguous.

Waypoint. Throws a TypeError on an opaque origin, counts kQuotaRead, then makes a single QuotaManagerHost::QueryStorageUsageAndQuota mojo call and resolves with whatever the browser returned. It computes nothing. A renderer-only patch here would be an accessor override in everything but name and would leave the browser process holding the real numbers, which the same origin can read back through chrome://quota-internals and DevTools' Storage pane.

Decides the *shape* of usageDetails rather than its numbers: only indexedDatabase, serviceWorkerCache, serviceWorker and fileSystem are copied out of the mojo UsageBreakdown, and each key is set only when its value is non-zero (lines 79-91). So an untouched origin gets usageDetails === {} with no keys at all, which is exactly what the capture shows. The key set is a Chromium-version constant, not a device property.

Waypoint, but the important one: it calls GetUsageAndReportedQuotaWithBreakdown, not GetUsageAndQuotaWithBreakdown. That is the fork between the number the page sees and the number the quota system actually enforces. GetUsageAndQuotaForDevtools (quota_manager_impl.cc:1224) takes the unfiltered path, so DevTools and the page legitimately disagree in stock Chrome.

Gated on report_static_storage_quota_ && !IsStorageUnlimited(storage_key). When the gate is open it discards the real per-storage-key quota computed by UsageAndQuotaInfoGatherer and substitutes CalculateReportedQuota(total_space, usage, is_incognito). When it is closed it falls through to the real value. Waypoint, but it is the switch that decides which of two emitters is the source.

THE source of navigator.storage.estimate().quota at this revision. Three lines of arithmetic and no disk query of its own: if total_space >= 10 * kGBytes it returns usage + 10 GiB (line 148-150); otherwise it returns usage + ceil(total_space / 1 GiB) * 1 GiB (lines 156-160). kGBytes = 1024^3 (quota_manager_impl.h:161). So the reported quota is a constant on every device with at least 10 GiB of *total* disk, it does not track free space, and it grows only with the origin's own usage. The pre-M110 'quota is a fraction of free disk' folk knowledge is stale and any patch written against it would introduce a leak rather than close one.

The bucket analogue of GetUsageAndReportedQuotaWithBreakdown, and it has one extra branch that matters: if bucket.quota > 0 - i.e. the page asked for an explicit quota in storageBuckets.open(name, {quota: N}) - that exact N is echoed back unchanged (lines 1316-1320), before CalculateReportedQuota is ever reached. A bucket estimate is therefore page-controlled and carries no device information; only the default-quota bucket falls through to the 10 GiB constant.

BASE_FEATURE(kStaticStorageQuota, base::FEATURE_ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT), commented in-tree as 'A kill switch for the new reported quota being a static value.' Enabled by default at this revision, which is why the capture reads exactly 10737418240 = 10 * 2^30. This flag, not the quota arithmetic, is the thing to watch across rebases: if it is ever flipped off, quota goes back to being 75% of a pool that is 80% of total disk and starts leaking the host volume again.

BASE_FEATURE(kIncognitoStaticStorageQuota, base::FEATURE_DISABLED_BY_DEFAULT), commented 'If enabled, Incognito mode will always report a maximal quota value to avoid fingerprinting and incognito detection.' Chromium has written the fix and left it off. With it off, incognito quota is derived from physical memory (see emit.storage.quota-settings-incognito) and is detectable on any machine with less than roughly 60 GiB of RAM.

Reads ContentBrowserClient::GetOverrideValueForStaticStorageQuota(browser_context) and falls back to the feature flag, then passes the result into QuotaContext. An embedder override point that exists before the feature flag is consulted - the cheapest place to force the static-quota behaviour on if a rebase ever flips the flag off, and the place a patch belongs rather than in CalculateReportedQuota itself.

The real (enforced) quota, and the only place total disk space enters the system: pool_size = total * kPoolSizeRatio (0.8), per_storage_key_quota = pool_size * 0.75, plus the should_remain_available / must_remain_available reserves. With kStaticStorageQuota enabled this value no longer reaches navigator.storage.estimate at all - it only decides when writes start failing. Marked source of truth because it is still observable indirectly: a page that writes until QuotaExceededError measures 60% of the host volume regardless of what estimate() claimed.

In incognito the pool is a fraction of *physical memory*, not of disk: pool_size = AmountOfPhysicalMemory() * U(0.15, 0.20) drawn once from base::RandDouble() with refresh_interval = TimeDelta::Max(), so it is fixed for the browser session and different on the next launch. Two consequences. (1) It leaks host RAM. (2) Fed to CalculateReportedQuota as total_space it produces a quota below 10 GiB on any machine with less than about 60 GiB of RAM - a 16 GiB laptop reports 3 or 4 GiB - which is a direct incognito tell and is also non-deterministic across sessions, violating axiom A3 for free.

The disk read. In the normal profile it posts CallGetVolumeInfo on the DB runner against profile_path_ and hands the raw base::SysInfo::DiskSpaceInfo to DidGetStorageCapacity. In incognito it short-circuits to ContinueIncognitoGetStorageCapacity (line 2695) which synthesises a fake DiskSpaceInfo whose total is the memory-derived pool size. So 'total disk space' as the quota system understands it means two entirely different quantities depending on profile type.

The source of both usage and the per-client breakdown: it fans out to every registered QuotaClient (IndexedDB, CacheStorage, ServiceWorker, FileSystem) and sums real on-disk bytes for the storage key. This is genuine site-caused state, starts at zero for an origin that has never been visited, and contains nothing about the host.

Not a storage query at all: it calls PermissionService::HasPermission with a PERSISTENT_STORAGE descriptor and resolves true iff the status is GRANTED. persisted() and navigator.permissions.query({name:'persistent-storage'}) therefore read the same browser-side bit through two different mojo interfaces and can never be made to disagree - which also means any patch to one that misses the other is immediately visible.

Copies the caller's StorageBucketOptions (persisted, quota, durability) into a BucketPolicies mojo struct with has_* flags, rejecting quota === 0 with a TypeError (line 132). Every value it sends is one the page just supplied; the browser decides what is honoured.

Per-bucket estimate. Note it resolves a StorageEstimate whose usageDetails is a freshly created, always-empty StorageUsageDetails (line 272-273) - unlike navigator.storage.estimate(), the bucket form never populates a breakdown. That asymmetry is stock behaviour and must be preserved.

Parses the descriptor, then calls PermissionService::HasPermission and wraps the mojo PermissionStatus in a PermissionStatus object. No state is decided here. The renderer holds no permission table at all, so a renderer-side patch would have to fabricate a value the browser would then contradict through Notification.permission, persisted(), an actual getUserMedia call and the PermissionStatus change event.

The source of which names are queryable and which throw. The IDL enum (permissions/permission_descriptor.idl:6) admits 44 names at this revision; this function then rejects a subset at runtime with a TypeError: 'ambient-light-sensor' unless SensorExtraClasses, 'geolocation-approximate', 'nfc', 'system-wake-lock', 'local-fonts', 'captured-surface-control' and 'speaker-selection' behind their own runtime flags, and 'keyboard-lock'/'pointer-lock' behind #if !IS_ANDROID && !IS_IOS. That last pair makes the accepted-name set platform-dependent and therefore a coherence constraint on the claimed OS. Note also that accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer all collapse to one PermissionName::SENSORS, so the three can never disagree.

The content-layer join point every permission read converges on, whatever API was used. It applies permissions-policy and devtools overrides and then delegates to the embedder's PermissionControllerDelegate. Waypoint - but it is the single choke point where the embedder is selected, and therefore where a headless build diverges from a headed one.

Converts a ContentSetting from HostContentSettingsMap into a PermissionStatus. For a fresh profile with no exceptions the map returns the registry default, so the default state map is decided one level down in content_settings_registry.cc - except where a subclass overrides GetContentSettingStatusInternal outright, which is how screen-wake-lock and clipboard-write end up granted with no entry in the map at all.

The source of the default permission state for every name that is backed by a content setting. Verified defaults at this revision: GEOLOCATION ASK (148), NOTIFICATIONS ASK (158), MEDIASTREAM_MIC ASK (172), MEDIASTREAM_CAMERA ASK (185), MIDI_SYSEX ASK (209), PERSISTENT_STORAGE/durable-storage ASK (235), BACKGROUND_SYNC ALLOW (246), SENSORS ALLOW (352), CLIPBOARD_READ_WRITE ASK (362), PAYMENT_HANDLER ALLOW (373). These are compile-time constants, identical on every platform and every fresh profile, and they reproduce the captured state map exactly.

Hard override, no content setting consulted: WAKE_LOCK_SCREEN returns CONTENT_SETTING_ALLOW and WAKE_LOCK_SYSTEM returns CONTENT_SETTING_BLOCK, unconditionally. So screen-wake-lock is always 'granted' and system-wake-lock - when its runtime flag is on - is always 'denied', on every platform, for every origin, and neither can be changed by the user. Two constants a detector can use as a liveness check on the whole permission stack.

Returns CONTENT_SETTING_ALLOW unconditionally (line 67) after giving the extensions delegate a chance to answer. This is why clipboard-write reads 'granted' while clipboard-read reads 'prompt' in the capture: they are two different ContentSettingsTypes, CLIPBOARD_SANITIZED_WRITE and CLIPBOARD_READ_WRITE, and only the latter is in the registry. A tool that spoofs both to the same value gets this pair wrong.

Returns blink::mojom::PermissionStatus::ASK for every permission, unconditionally - as do GetPermissionResultForCurrentDocument (59), ForWorker (67) and ForEmbeddedRequester (75). Constructed only by headless/lib/browser/headless_browser_context_impl.cc:62, i.e. only in the chrome-headless-shell binary. The consequence is a seven-name discriminator: background-sync, clipboard-write, accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, screen-wake-lock and payment-handler all read 'prompt' there and 'granted' in any headed or --headless=new Chrome. This is a far wider tell than the Notification.permission one it is usually reduced to, and it cannot be fixed inside this subsystem: it is a choice of binary.

Mostly a forwarder to NotificationManager::GetPermissionStatus (a synchronous mojo call), but it adds two renderer-side rewrites that the Permissions API does not have: 'denied' for any non-secure context without any IPC at all (line 423-425), and ASK downgraded to DENIED when the frame is cross-origin to the outermost main frame (lines 444-449). So Notification.permission and permissions.query legitimately disagree inside a cross-origin iframe on http - a detector that treats disagreement as proof of automation is wrong there, and one that treats agreement in a top-level https frame as guaranteed is right.

The source, and the exact mechanism of the classic headless tell. Lines 127-131: if the BrowserContext has no PlatformNotificationService the call returns DENIED without ever consulting the permission controller. Only when a service exists does it fall through to CheckPermissionStatus (line 239) which asks the same PermissionController the Permissions API uses.

return nullptr;. Combined with blink_notification_service_impl.cc:127 this makes Notification.permission === 'denied' in chrome-headless-shell, while HeadlessPermissionManager::GetPermissionStatus makes navigator.permissions.query({name:'notifications'}).state === 'prompt'. The two reads disagree, in a top-level secure context where they must agree. That is the tell named in docs/SUBSYSTEMS.md section 11, located precisely, and still live at this revision.

Returns voice_list_, a renderer-side cache filled by OnSetVoiceList (line 85) when the browser pushes the list over mojo. The first synchronous call after page load usually returns an empty array because the push has not arrived - the voiceschanged race the collector works around - so 'getVoices() is empty' is not by itself evidence of anything. The cache holds no logic; every field is a straight read of the mojo struct (speech_synthesis_voice.h:44-48).

The translation layer, and it is where two observable properties are manufactured rather than read: out_voice->voice_uri = voices[i].name (so voiceURI is always a byte-copy of name and the real platform identifier, e.g. com.apple.voice.compact.en-US.Samantha, is never exposed) and out_voice->is_default = (i == 0) (so exactly one voice is default and it is whichever the platform layer put first). Any synthesised voice list that gives voiceURI a distinct value, or marks a non-first entry default, is generating a shape this code cannot produce.

Concatenates platform voices from TtsPlatformImpl::GetVoices with engine (extension) voices from the TtsEngineDelegate. On stock Chrome with no TTS extension installed the second source is empty, which is why the capture contains only Apple system voices and no 'Google ...' remote entries. A profile that claims a machine with the Google TTS extension would need entries with localService false, and there are none in this list.

The source on macOS, and it explains every structural feature of the captured 86-entry list. AVSpeechSynthesisVoice.speechVoices sorted by name ascending (125-127); the system default voice removed and re-inserted at index 0 (128-131), which is how Samantha becomes default:true; a name-collision count (141-157) that appends a localised language in parentheses when a name repeats, producing the 'Eddy (English (United States))' form; data.native = true for every entry (184), which is why localService is true throughout. The list is therefore a function of the macOS version, the installed voice packs and the user's default-voice and locale settings - exactly the OS-specific resource set docs/SUBSYSTEMS.md section 12 warns about.

Compile-time platform switch selecting the concrete provider: Mac, Android, Win (WinRT or the legacy COM stack), ChromeOS, Linux+udev, and no provider at all otherwise. The Device Service runs in-process in the browser for Chrome, so this is browser-process code despite living under services/. Nothing about the claimed platform can change which branch was compiled in.

std::move(callback).Run(nullptr); for every sensor type, with an in-tree comment saying the hardware pokes stopped working long ago and 'there is nothing available'. So on macOS every Accelerometer/Gyroscope/OrientationSensor.start() fails at the provider, and no macOS Chrome has ever produced a generic-sensor reading. This is a positive, checkable macOS signature rather than an absence: a machine claiming macOS that returns real accelerometer readings is not macOS.

Turns a failed creation into the observable: SensorCreationResult::ERROR_NOT_ALLOWED becomes a NotAllowedError, anything else - including the macOS 'no provider' nullptr - becomes a NotReadableError delivered as a SensorErrorEvent on the sensor object. NotAllowedError vs NotReadableError is therefore a two-way discriminator between 'permission refused' and 'no such hardware', and a detector reads it from one error event.

DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission() and DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission() resolve to the state of PermissionName::SENSORS, whose registry default is ALLOW. So on desktop Chrome the static requestPermission() resolves 'granted' with no prompt and no user gesture - unlike iOS Safari, where it is a real gate - and in chrome-headless-shell it resolves 'prompt'. The method exists on every platform because DeviceOrientationRequestPermission is status:stable in runtime_enabled_features.json5:2303.

The source on macOS. Reads IOPowerSources: charging = !on_battery_power || is_charging; level = current_capacity / max_capacity as a raw unrounded double; charging_time and discharging_time = base::Minutes(k).InSeconds() from kIOPSTimeToFullChargeKey / kIOPSTimeToEmptyKey, so both are always exact multiples of 60 and Infinity when unknown. The captured chargingTime 5160 is 86 minutes, which fits. level is NOT bucketed by Chromium, so it is a high-entropy real number - but it moves continuously on real hardware, which is why it reads as device state.

charging = true, charging_time = 0.0, discharging_time = INFINITY, level = 1.0. Any platform without a working BatteryStatusManager - battery_status_manager_default.cc:38 on Fuchsia and anything not covered by services/device/battery/BUILD.gn:36-71, or Linux where UPower reports no battery device - never overwrites these, so getBattery() resolves exactly {charging:true, level:1, chargingTime:0, dischargingTime:Infinity}. That tuple is the canonical 'this is a desktop, a VM or a server' signature. It is also entirely legitimate for a real iMac, Mac Studio or desktop PC, which is what makes it a profile-consistency question rather than a patch.

Straight reads of a cached BatteryStatus pushed from the device service via BatteryDispatcher (battery_dispatcher.cc:34-35), with no rounding, clamping or quantisation anywhere in the renderer. BatteryManager is [SecureContext] and Exposed=Window only, so navigator.getBattery is absent on http and in workers - an availability difference that is stock behaviour and must not be smoothed over.

The source of the plugin list's *contents*, as opposed to the one bit that decides whether it exists. When IsPdfViewerAvailable() is true the constructor synthesises five DOMPlugin objects from a hard-coded Vector<String>{'PDF Viewer', 'Chrome PDF Viewer', 'Chromium PDF Viewer', 'Microsoft Edge PDF Viewer', 'WebKit built-in PDF'} (lines 60-65), each with filename 'internal-pdf-viewer', description 'Portable Document Format' and the two mime types application/pdf and text/pdf with suffixes 'pdf' (MakeFakePlugin, lines 40-51). Nothing about the host reaches any of these strings; the in-tree comment (57-59) says outright that the list is spec-fixed to reduce fingerprinting. The captured list is byte-identical to it.

navigator.mimeTypes is not an independent list: the constructor takes DOMPluginArray::GetFixedMimeTypeArray() (dom_plugin_array.cc:127), which returns the two DOMMimeType objects belonging to plugins[0] - the same objects, not copies. So navigator.mimeTypes[0].enabledPlugin === navigator.plugins[0], navigator.mimeTypes.length is 2 whenever navigator.plugins.length is 5 and 0 whenever it is 0, and there is a DCHECK (dom_plugin_array.cc:131) asserting plugins[0] has exactly two mime types. Three observables, one bit; a fabricated list that gets the object identity wrong is detectable with ===.

The one runtime input to the whole plugin surface: when prefs::kPluginsAlwaysOpenPdfExternally is true (the 'Download PDFs instead of automatically opening them' setting, or the AlwaysOpenPdfExternally enterprise policy) the PDF extension is excluded, application/pdf leaves PluginData, and navigator.plugins becomes empty with pdfViewerEnabled false. Real users do have this set, so an empty plugin list is not proof of a spoof - but for a profile that claims the default configuration it is a mismatch, and it is decided in the browser process where a renderer-side patch cannot see it.

The source of every CSS system colour on macOS except Highlight and HighlightText, and of all of them on Linux. A flat table of constants keyed only on dark_mode: ActiveText 0xFF0000, GrayText 0x808080, and in dark mode BtnFace 0x6B6B6B, BtnText white, Field 0x3B3B3B, FieldText white, Scrollbar/Window 0x121212, WindowText white, LinkText/Hotlight 0x9E9EFF, VisitedText 0xD0ADF0. Every one of these reproduces the captured dark-mode value exactly. No OS query is involved.

On macOS the native mapping covers exactly two colours and both are hard-coded: kColorCssSystemHighlight = 0xB3D7FF and kColorCssSystemHighlightText = black. The comment says the real NSColor.selectedTextBackgroundColor is deliberately not used 'due to fingerprinting concerns' (crbug.com/436597797), so the user's macOS accent colour does not leak. LayoutTheme then runs BlendWithWhite over it (layout_theme.cc:868), which converts the opaque 0xB3D7FF into the captured rgba(179, 215, 255, 0.8). This is the one file that makes the macOS colour set different from the Linux one, and it is compiled in by platform, not selected at runtime.

The opposite case, and the reason this surface cannot simply be inherited. On Windows, in light mode or under forced colors, ten CSS system colours are wired straight to the kColorNative* ids that NativeThemeWin fills from GetSysColor - real, user-customisable OS values. In dark mode without forced colors the branch is skipped and the generic constants stand. So a Windows profile served from a macOS or Linux host emits the generic table where real Windows emits GetSysColor output, and a Windows host serving a macOS profile emits the user's Windows palette where macOS would emit constants.

Dispatches on ColorProviderKey::forced_colors: kNone and kSystem take CompleteDefaultCssSystemColorDefinition followed by the per-platform native mapping; the five named high-contrast themes (Dusk, Desert, NightSky, Aquatic, White) replace the whole table with their own literals. A profile reporting forced-colors: none must not emit any of those five palettes, and the capture confirms forced-colors: none with the generic table.

The cross-process hop. The browser builds three ui::RendererColorMaps - light, dark and forced - with ui::CreateRendererColorMap (line 615) and ships them to the renderer in CreateViewParams (render_view_host_impl.cc:447) and on every UpdateColorProviders (blink/public/mojom/page/page.mojom:177). This is why css.system-colors is a multi-process surface: the values are computed in the browser from the platform mixers, and the renderer only looks them up. A Blink-only patch would leave the browser's own UI and any later UpdateColorProviders push disagreeing with what the page sees.

The lookup, reached from StyleColor::ResolveSystemColor (style_color.cc:495) and therefore from getComputedStyle as well as from painting. It maps 38 CSS keywords onto 11 ui::kColorCssSystem* ids - most of the deprecated names collapse together, e.g. ActiveBorder, InactiveBorder, ThreeDDarkShadow, ThreeDHighlight, ThreeDLightShadow, ThreeDShadow and WindowFrame all become kColorCssSystemBtnText, which is why all seven read rgb(255,255,255) in the dark-mode capture rather than the 0x6B6B6B they would get from the fallback path. Keywords with no case here (Mark, MarkText, AccentColor) fall through to DefaultSystemColor.

The fallback table, and the source for the keywords the provider switch does not handle: Mark 0xFFFF00 and MarkText 0x000000 (lines 728-731), both matching the capture, plus AccentColor / AccentColorText behind CSSAccentColorKeywordEnabled. It is also the source for *all* 38 colours when color_provider is null - which is the case in web tests and in any renderer that never received the colour maps. Its dark-mode values differ from the provider's for the ButtonBorder family (0x6B6B6B vs white), so 'ActiveBorder is grey in dark mode' is a positive signal that the colour-map plumbing did not run.

The sample rate of an offline render is the constructor argument, validated against IsValidAudioBufferSampleRate (3000..768000) and used verbatim. There is no default and no hardware query anywhere on this path, which is what makes the offline render independent of the audio device.

Returns channel_count_, the constructor value. Contrast realtime_audio_destination_handler.cc:209, which returns the hardware count - the two destinations answer the same JS property from completely different sources.

Constructs FFTFrame frame(fft_size) at :432 and calls frame.DoInverseFFT(data_span) at :479 once per pitch range. Every sample a 'triangle', 'square', 'sawtooth' or custom oscillator emits is read out of a table produced here, so the FFT backend is upstream of the entire oscillator output. GenerateBasicWaveform at :497-572 supplies only the Fourier coefficients and uses no libm - b = 2*(pi_factor*pi_factor)*sign for the triangle - so the coefficients are exact and all the divergence is in the transform.
A dispatcher, not a source: if rust_fft_ has a value it delegates to RustFFT, otherwise to PlatformDoInverseFFT. Patching here would be patching a switch statement.

rust_fft_ = blink::rust_fft::rustfft_new(fft_size_) when the WebAudioRustFft feature is on. The feature is status:"stable" at runtime_enabled_features.json5:6979-6980, so this is the default in a stable 152 build, and --disable-blink-features=WebAudioRustFft flips the whole engine back to vDSP-on-Mac or PFFFT-elsewhere. That switch is the only deterministic, A3-compatible lever we have over the render.

THE RUNTIME CPU DISPATCH. Tries FftPlannerAvx, then FftPlannerSse, then FftPlannerNeon, then FftPlannerWasmSimd, then FftPlannerScalar. avx_planner.rs:124-126 requires both is_x86_feature_detected!("avx") and ("fma"); neon_planner.rs:156 checks is_aarch64_feature_detected!("neon"). third_party/rust/rustfft/v6/BUILD.gn:91-95 compiles all of avx, sse and neon in. The result is that the arithmetic performed on a page's audio graph is chosen by CPUID at the first FFT, not by anything in the profile.
Fused multiply-add: one rounding per butterfly term. Selected only when the host CPU reports AVX and FMA.

_mm_add_ps(acc, _mm_mul_ps(a, b)) - two roundings where the AVX kernel has one. This is the concrete reason an x86 host without FMA renders different bytes from an x86 host with it, on the same binary.
vfmaq_f32 is an explicitly fused intrinsic, so -ffp-contract=off does not unfuse it. Rounds like the AVX path, not like the SSE path.

The pre-RustFFT Mac backend: Apple Accelerate. vDSP_create_fftsetup at :62, vDSP_fft_zrip forward at :138 and inverse at :154. Compiled only when is_mac (third_party/blink/renderer/platform/BUILD.gn:1744) and reached only when WebAudioRustFft is off. Its results are an OS library's, so they can move with a macOS update without any Chromium change.

The pre-RustFFT non-Mac backend, guarded by #if !BUILDFLAG(IS_MAC) at :7 through :232 and listed unconditionally at platform/BUILD.gn:449. Bundled source rather than a system library, so it is at least stable across OS versions - but it is a different transform from vDSP, which is why the Mac and non-Mac renders differed before RustFFT landed.

Compiled when current_cpu is x86 or x64 (webaudio/BUILD.gn:182-184). Advances the wavetable phase in __m128 SINGLE precision and says so at :115-117 - 'Ideally, to preserve accuracy, we should use (two) packed double vectors for this, but that degrades performance quite a bit' - and again at :188, 'There's a bit of round-off above'. The scalar fallback advances the same phase in double. The divergence is documented in Chromium's own comments.

Compiled when current_cpu is arm, arm64 or arm64e (webaudio/BUILD.gn:186-189). Uses vmlaq_f32 for the two interpolation steps at :234, :240 and :247 where the SSE2 file uses separate _mm_mul_ps and _mm_add_ps. With -ffp-contract=off clang should lower vmlaq_f32 unfused, which would make the two kernels agree - but that is an inference about clang's arm_neon.h lowering, not a verified fact, and it is one of the things the cross-architecture capture named in audio.offline-render would settle.

The #if !(ARCH_CPU_X86_FAMILY || CPU_ARM_NEON) fallbacks at :354-364 and :368-421. ProcessKRateVector here returns 0 and defers everything to ProcessKRateScalar, which carries the phase in double throughout - a third arithmetic behaviour distinct from both SIMD kernels.

THE OS DEPENDENCE, call site 1. sin(static_cast<double>(kPiOverTwoFloat * compressor_gain)) - unqualified, so it binds to the host libm from <cmath>, not to fdlibm, even though the same file includes third_party/fdlibm/ieee754.h and calls fdlibm::powf at :145 and fdlibm::asinf at :190. Evaluated once per division frame (kNumberOfDivisionFrames = 32) for the whole render.

THE OS DEPENDENCE, call site 2. exp(static_cast<double>(-k * (x - linear_threshold_))) - again unqualified host libm. KneeCurve is also called fifteen times per parameter update inside the k-search loop at :529-552, so a last-ULP difference here changes the compression curve constant k itself, not just one sample.

THE OS DEPENDENCE, call sites 3 and 4, and the ones that matter most. powf(10, 0.05f*decibels) at :38 and 20*log10f(linear) at :44 - both unqualified host-libm FLOAT functions, in a file that includes fdlibm and uses fdlibm::exp at :69. LinearToDecibels runs on the compressor's per-sample metering path (dynamics_compressor.cc:337) and inside Saturate; because metering_gain_ feeds db_compression_diff feeds envelope_rate feeds compressor_gain, a 1-ULP float difference here is amplified by the compressor's own feedback loop rather than absorbed. Unlike the sin and exp sites there is no double-to-float truncation to hide it.

namespace impl = mac (Accelerate) / neon / x86 / scalar, chosen by #if at :34-56. For the two operations the oscillator table path uses - Vsmul at periodic_wave.cc:447,:452,:493 and Vmaxmgv at :484 - every backend is exactly rounded per element, so this split does NOT by itself change the render. Recorded as a source of truth anyway because it does change order-dependent reductions elsewhere in the graph, and because it is the obvious wrong place to look for the divergence.

static const bool supports = ::base::CPU().has_avx() - a second, independent runtime CPU dispatch, this one inside Blink rather than inside rustfft, choosing between the AVX and SSE vector kernels at :61-64, :104 and :125. Same class of problem as the rustfft planner.

x86 sets MXCSR bits 0x8040 (FTZ | DAZ) at :63; ARM sets FPCR bit 24 (FZ) at :108; Windows uses _controlfp_s(_DN_FLUSH) at :85. Broadly equivalent but not identical in edge cases - x86 DAZ zeroes denormal INPUTS while ARM FZ has its own input rules - so the two architectures can disagree on samples that decay into the denormal range, which is exactly what the tail of a compressor release does.

Applied unconditionally under is_clang at :656-661. This is the fact that BOUNDS the problem: the compiler never fuses a*b+c on its own, so compiler-introduced FMA divergence is ruled out and only explicit FMA intrinsics (rustfft AVX, rustfft NEON, possibly vmlaq_f32) and the host libm remain. Recorded as an emitter because a build-configuration change here would silently change every audio render in the fork.
return destination_handler_->SampleRate() - the JS accessor, and a pure relay. Patching it would be an A1 violation with a two-line diff, which is exactly why it is worth marking as not a source.

context_sample_rate_ = the AudioContextOptions sampleRate when supplied, else web_audio_device_->SampleRate(). Note :567-572: when the two differ, Blink inserts a resampler with scale_factor = context_sample_rate_ / web_audio_device_->SampleRate(). Chromium therefore already has the machinery to run a context at a rate the hardware does not support.
return current_sink_params_.sample_rate() - the renderer's copy of media::AudioParameters obtained from the browser.

AudioDeviceFactory::GetInstance()->GetOutputDeviceInfo(frame_token, device_id).output_params() - THE PROCESS BOUNDARY. Everything above this line is renderer, everything below is browser and audio service.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the sample rate, channel count and buffer size a page eventually reads. Runs in the AUDIO SERVICE. This is the audio equivalent of the deviceMemory / DPR / Accept-Language duplications: the value is computed in a process the renderer patch cannot see, and only a copy reaches JavaScript.

AudioObjectGetPropertyData(kAudioDevicePropertyNominalSampleRate) - a live CoreAudio query, falling back to kFallbackSampleRate = 44100 (:76) on failure. The 48000 in our capture is the M4 Max's nominal output rate, read from the OS.

For output, 2 * media::limits::kMinAudioBufferSize = 2 * 128 = 256 (media/base/limits.h:83), then adjusted by GetMinAudioBufferSizeMacOS. 256/48000 is exactly the measured baseLatency of 0.005333333333333333.

THE EXISTING LEVER. Reads --audio-buffer-size (media/base/media_switches.cc:53) and overrides ChooseBufferSize outright. A profile can set baseLatency to any frame count with a launch switch and no patch at all - the same class of mechanism as the GPU shard's driver-bug-workaround switches, and it belongs in the profile loader rather than in a patch series.

Marked a source of truth for the ARITHMETIC - the two inputs come from elsewhere, but the max() and the division happen here, so a fork that changes only the audio-service buffer size still gets a consistent answer out of this line.
return web_audio_device_->FramesPerBuffer() - a relay of the audio service's frames_per_buffer.

std::round(output_position_.hardware_output_latency / factor) * factor, where factor is kOutputLatencyQuatizingFactor = 0.008 without microphone permission and kOutputLatencyMaxPrecisionFactor = 0.001 with it (:83-89). The privacy mitigation is already in stock Chrome; the permission-dependent precision is the part that has to stay coherent with permissions.query.
Reports the autoplay-gated context state. Not a device value - it moved between 'suspended' and 'running' across four captures on one machine.
return GetAudioDestinationHandler().MaxChannelCount() - one accessor over two completely different handlers, realtime and offline.
return platform_destination_->MaxChannelCount().

return original_sink_params_.channels() - deliberately the UNSCALED hardware parameters, so unlike SampleRate() this one cannot be moved by an AudioContextOptions override. The only way to change it is at the audio service.
fftSize = 2048, maxDecibels = -30, minDecibels = -100, smoothingTimeConstant = 0.8.

A mojo request out of the renderer with a 4-second timeout (:88). The renderer holds no device list.
Browser-process hop into MediaStreamManager's MediaDevicesManager; also where label suppression for un-permissioned callers is applied.
audio_system_->GetDeviceDescriptions - THE SECOND PROCESS BOUNDARY on this path, from browser into the audio service (services/audio/system_info.cc:56-62).

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the audiooutput entries, enumerated from CoreAudio in the audio service. AudioManagerBase::GetAudioDeviceDescriptions at audio_manager_base.cc:343 wraps it. Patching here makes enumerateDevices, getUserMedia and MediaStreamTrack.getSettings all agree by construction.

Every member defaults to true; the [RuntimeEnabled=MediaCaptureBackgroundBlur] and [RuntimeEnabled=MediaCaptureCameraControls] members at :50-53 are the only ones that can be absent, which is exactly the difference visible in our capture.

A serialiser over webrtc::RtpCapabilities. Worth noting that sdpFmtpLine is ASSEMBLED here at :300-311 by joining the parameter map with ';' - so the exact string a detector reads is Chromium's formatting of libwebrtc's data, and its key order is the map's.
Same serialiser shape as the receiver, over GetSenderCapabilities at :1031.

GetPcFactory()->GetRtpSenderCapabilities / GetRtpReceiverCapabilities at :1306-1327. The factory was constructed with encoder and decoder factories that wrap media::GpuVideoAcceleratorFactories, so the hardware term enters here.

auto profiles = gpu_factories->GetVideoEncodeAcceleratorSupportedProfiles() at :300 - the hardware encoder list, plus software fallbacks. This is why the sender's video codec list is shorter, differently ordered, and carries different H265 level-ids than the receiver's.
The decoder-side counterpart, also built over media::GpuVideoAcceleratorFactories. Together with the encoder factory it is why the receiver's video codec list is broader than the sender's.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the WebRTC sender's video codec list. GetSupportedProfilesInternal at :231-320 asks each platform VEA for vea->GetSupportedProfiles() and is additionally filtered by gpu_preferences and gpu_workarounds - the same workaround table gpu.angle-backend already establishes is keyed on GPUInfo, which is what makes this patchable from the same place as the GPU claim rather than needing its own mechanism.

THE ORIGIN OF EVERY LOCAL ADDRESS WEBRTC CAN SEE, on macOS and POSIX: a getifaddrs(3) walk producing name, friendly_name, interface_index, ConnectionType, IPAddress, prefix_length, ip_address_attributes and an optional EUI-48 MAC per interface. No proxy configuration is consulted or consultable here - it is a kernel query.

SOURCE OF TRUTH and the recommended patch point for the whole shard. Runs in the network service on network_list_task_runner_, called from OnNetworkChanged (:205-221) and from StartNetworkNotifications (:387). Replacing the list here means the renderer never receives the host's real interface names or MAC addresses at all, and the mDNS, filtering, priority and SDP layers all follow by construction.

SECOND SOURCE OF TRUTH, and easy to miss. Creates a DatagramClientSocket from url_request_context_->GetNetworkSessionContext()->client_socket_factory - NOT the proxy-resolving factory - and ConnectAsync-es it to the hardcoded 8.8.8.8:53 or 2001:4860:4860::8888:53 (constants at :46-49) purely to read back GetLocalAddress(). This value becomes the host candidate whenever adapter enumeration is off, so patching DoGetNetworkList without patching this leaves the real default address exposed in exactly the modes that are supposed to hide it.

THE PROCESS BOUNDARY. Receives the full Vector<net::NetworkInterface> plus both default local addresses over the mojom::P2PNetworkNotificationClient pipe and fans it out to every NetworkListObserver. A pure relay, but the point at which the renderer gains a complete copy of the host's network topology.

Converts net::NetworkInterface to webrtc::Network. Two decisions are taken here that are observable downstream: the adapter type, from it->type falling back to GetAdapterTypeFromName(it->name) at :126-128, and the VPN flag, from IsVpnMacAddress(*it->mac_address) at :130-135. Both feed network cost and therefore candidate priority. IPv6 addresses that are MAC-based, deprecated, link-local or loopback are dropped at :155-160.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for how the IP handling policy becomes behaviour. The switch at :1090-1111 turns the four modes into three booleans, and :1128-1134 chooses FilteringNetworkManager when enable_multiple_routes is set and EmptyNetworkManager otherwise. Also the point where mic/camera permission enters WebRTC at all, via GetWebRTCMediaPermission at :1121-1124. Note :1074 - if the embedder returns false from ShouldEnforceWebRTCRoutingPreferences the entire policy is skipped and both booleans are forced true.

The three-line translation that is the real content of the IP handling policy: !enable_multiple_routes -> PORTALLOCATOR_DISABLE_ADAPTER_ENUMERATION; !enable_default_local_candidate -> PORTALLOCATOR_DISABLE_DEFAULT_LOCAL_CANDIDATE; !enable_nonproxied_udp -> DISABLE_UDP | DISABLE_STUN | DISABLE_UDP_RELAY together. set_allow_tcp_listen(false) at :48 is unconditional, which is why Chromium never emits passive TCP host candidates.

Returns an empty vector unless enumeration_permission() == ENUMERATION_ALLOWED, which happens only after microphone or camera permission is granted (OnPermissionStatus at :151-167). It is a filter over IpcNetworkManager's list, not a producer - but note :169-203, where it copies the networks and unconditionally installs the real default local addresses via set_default_local_addresses, so the default address survives the filtering.

Returns {} and sets ENUMERATION_BLOCKED in the constructor at :28 - but GetDefaultLocalAddress at :67-74 forwards straight through to IpcNetworkManager, so the three non-default IP handling modes still know the machine's default local address even though they enumerate nothing. That forwarding is what makes default_public_and_private_interfaces able to emit one private address.

Converts ENUMERATION_BLOCKED into PORTALLOCATOR_DISABLE_ADAPTER_ENUMERATION at :674-677, then substitutes GetAnyAddressNetworks() - a single 0.0.0.0 and a single :: - at :682-683. The comment at :678-681 is the clearest statement in the tree of the mistaken assumption this shard exists to record: binding to ANY reuses 'the same routing for http traffic by OS', which is the host's routing table and not the configured proxy.

Returns immediately on PORTALLOCATOR_DISABLE_UDP, which is how disable_non_proxied_udp erases every UDP candidate. Passes emit_local_candidate_for_anyaddress = !PORTALLOCATOR_DISABLE_DEFAULT_LOCAL_CANDIDATE into UDPPort::Create, which is the single boolean separating default_public_and_private_interfaces from default_public_interface_only.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the host candidate. Calls MaybeSetDefaultLocalAddress (:529-544) to swap an ANY-bound socket's address for the default local address, then AddAddress with IceCandidateType::kHost. If the default address lookup fails the ANY address is kept rather than the candidate dropped.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the server-reflexive candidate: AddAddress(stun_reflected_addr, ..., IceCandidateType::kSrflx, ...) at :577-579, where stun_reflected_addr is the MAPPED-ADDRESS the STUN server reported. The related address is stamped with the local address and emptied if MaybeSetDefaultLocalAddress fails (:568-572), so libwebrtc guards the LOCAL address here while emitting the PUBLIC one verbatim.

Where a Candidate is actually constructed. Stamps network_->id() and network_cost_ into the candidate at :224, computes the foundation from the base address and the ICE tiebreaker at :227, and sets the priority from type preference and network_->preference() at :229-232. Every one of those four fields survives mDNS sanitisation.

Substitutes the hostname for local and prflx candidates when mDNS is on, and empties related addresses under the conditions at :323-335. The MdnsResponderAdapter is constructed on the main thread only when BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_MDNS) and blink::features::kWebRtcHideLocalIpsWithMdns are both on, then moved onto the network thread into IpcNetworkManager at :1195-1202. If either is off the responder is null and every host candidate carries a raw IP.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for whether obfuscation happens on any given peer connection. The first condition is satisfied by a single grant of microphone OR camera permission, so mDNS is a pre-permission protection only.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the .local name. Appends '.local' to the generated name, caches the name-to-address mapping for the life of this responder, and schedules real multicast announcements on every interface (kMinNumAnnouncementsToSend, one second apart). Two calls for the same address in one responder return the same name.

base::Uuid::GenerateRandomV4().AsLowercaseString(). Installed as the default generator at :830. No device, profile or session entropy reaches the name, which is why webrtc.host-candidate-mdns is inherit rather than spoof.

THE PROXY FORK, in six lines. P2P_SOCKET_UDP constructs a P2PSocketUdp that is never handed the ProxyResolvingClientSocketFactory*; every TCP, SSLTCP and TLS variant, plain or STUN_, constructs a P2PSocketTcp or P2PSocketStunTcp that is. Whether WebRTC honours --proxy-server is decided entirely by which branch of this switch a candidate needs. Still literally true after patch 0086 — the UDP branch gets no ProxyResolvingClientSocketFactory — but the conclusion drawn from it no longer holds: the branch now receives a datagram socket factory that may already be proxy-bound, so which branch a candidate needs no longer decides whether WebRTC honours the proxy. See emit.network.p2p-socket-manager-resolve-udp-egress.

SOURCE OF TRUTH FOR THE PROXY BYPASS. The file contains no reference to any proxy type. Binds a plain net::UDPSocket - port 0 to the OS ephemeral range when no range is configured (:249-250), or the lowest free port ascending from min_port when one is (:251-257) - and sends STUN, TURN and media datagrams directly. That was the whole story until patches 0079 and 0086: the socket is now whatever P2PSocketManager's datagram factory produced, so under a single-hop SOCKS5 proxy it is a net::SOCKS5DatagramServerSocket relaying through a UDP ASSOCIATE, and under a proxy that cannot carry datagrams there is no socket at all. Direct egress over the host's real route is now one of three outcomes rather than the only one.

The proxied half of the fork: builds the connection through proxy_resolving_socket_factory_->CreateSocket(GURL("https://" + host:port), ...) at :115-117, deliberately passing the hostname rather than a resolved IP (:98-104) so the proxy resolves it. Wraps the result in a FakeSSLClientSocket for the pseudo-TLS variants. So TCP STUN and TCP/TLS TURN traverse the configured proxy correctly.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the claim that TCP-based ICE traffic is proxied. Calls the network session's proxy_resolution_service()->ResolveProxy, and DoProxyResolveComplete at :252-273 retains SCHEME_HTTP | SCHEME_HTTPS | SCHEME_SOCKS4 | SCHEME_SOCKS5 while dropping only SCHEME_QUIC. Connects with force_tunnel=true.

Maps libwebrtc's transport request onto the P2PSocketType enum: PROTO_SSLTCP -> STUN_SSLTCP/SSLTCP, PROTO_TLS -> STUN_TLS/TLS, otherwise STUN_TCP/TCP. CreateUdpSocket at :805 is the UDP counterpart and always requests P2P_SOCKET_UDP. This is where the choice that determines proxy participation is actually made, by protocol rather than by policy.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the stock default: RegisterStringPref(prefs::kWebRTCIPHandlingPolicy, blink::kWebRTCIPHandlingDefault) - the string 'default', i.e. full adapter enumeration and non-proxied UDP allowed. The pref name itself is chrome/common/pref_names.h:1112. The --webrtc-ip-handling-policy switch reaches it through chrome/browser/prefs/chrome_command_line_pref_store.cc:55.

Everything WebRTC's routing behaviour depends on crosses into the renderer through this one struct.

A relay, but the one place where a per-origin WebRTC policy could be expressed.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the interface ranking that ends up in every candidate's priority: sorts the merged list with SortNetworks and then assigns preference 127, 126, 125 ... descending at :529-538. Network ids are handed out sequentially at :468. Both are pure functions of the interface list, which is why patching the list in the network service is sufficient and patching anything here is not necessary.

ComputeNetworkCostByType (:112-164) maps adapter type to the constants in network_constants.h:22-58 - ethernet 0, wifi 10, unknown 50, 5G 250, 4G 500, cellular 900, 3G 910, 2G 980, 'any' 999 - plus 1 if the network is a VPN. That integer is emitted verbatim into the SDP candidate line, so link type and VPN presence are readable without any address.

local_preference = ((network_adapter_preference << 8) | IPAddressPrecedence(addr)) + relay_preference, and priority packs it between the type preference and the component id. Since network_adapter_preference is (127 - interface rank), the rank - and hence the interface count - is recoverable by arithmetic from any candidate's priority.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the wire form. Appends ' network-id <id>' when network_id() > 0 and ' network-cost <cost>' when network_cost() > 0 to the a=candidate line that RTCIceCandidate.candidate exposes verbatim to JavaScript. Nothing downstream strips them - Candidate::ToSanitizedCopy at :537 leaves both untouched.

KeyParams key_params = KeyParams(); - the default-constructed value, used whenever the application passes no certificate, which is every ordinary RTCPeerConnection. Generated asynchronously per connection, so the a=fingerprint bytes are fresh each time.

KT_DEFAULT is KT_ECDSA (ssl_identity.h:31), so the default certificate is ECDSA on EC_NIST_P256. Lifetime constants at ssl_identity.h:40-44: 30 days forward, 1 day backdated. These are the only version-dependent, device-independent facts an offer's a=fingerprint line and generateCertificate().expires expose.

CreateRandomString(ICE_UFRAG_LENGTH) and CreateRandomString(ICE_PWD_LENGTH), with the constants fixed at 4 and 24 in p2p_constants.cc:30,33. The 4/24 length pair is a libwebrtc signature visible in every offer and in every candidate's ufrag extension.

A three-branch mapping of webrtc::PeerConnectionInterface::IceGatheringState onto the IDL enum. The only writer is DidChangeIceGatheringState (:2617) via ChangeIceGatheringState (:2927) - the renderer holds no gathering state of its own.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for every deviceId and groupId a page sees: HMAC-SHA256 keyed by the requesting origin's serialisation, over raw_device_id followed by either device_id_salt or group_id_salt, hex-encoded lowercase to 64 characters. The early return at :243-247 passes empty, 'default' and 'communications' through unhashed, which is the only plaintext device id that ever reaches JavaScript.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the salting asymmetry. device_id_salt = salt, plus the per-document frame_salt only when are_persistent_device_ids_allowed is false; group_id_salt = salt + frame_salt + "group_id" unconditionally. So groupId always rotates on navigation while deviceId rotates only when cookies are blocked for that site.

Persistent device ids are allowed if and only if cookie_settings->IsFullCookieAccessAllowed for the frame (:7853-7859). When allowed the salt comes from MediaDeviceSaltService keyed by storage key; when not, the ephemeral BrowserContext::UniqueId() is used instead (:7866-7870). Clearing cookies clears the salt, which rotates every deviceId for that site.

The per-document frame salt, a fresh base::UnguessableToken (initialised at :2599, regenerated here on every committed navigation). It is the term that makes groupId per-document, and deviceId per-document too whenever cookies are blocked.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the pre-permission shape: without permission it returns WebMediaDeviceInfo with empty deviceId, empty label and empty groupId and a default VideoCaptureControlSupport. This is where the measured hasLabels:false is produced, and it is produced in the browser process - nothing in the renderer can be patched to reproduce it correctly.

`if (!has_permissions[i] && !translation[i].empty()) break;` - without permission exactly ONE entry per kind is emitted no matter how many devices exist. The same rule is written again at media_devices_util.cc:191-193. This is why the measured pre-permission counts of {1,1,1} are a constant rather than a property of the M4 Max, and it qualifies the corpus coverage of media.device-counts.
Returns the string the browser process sent. toJSON at :78 serialises deviceId, kind, label and groupId, so a detector gets all four in one call.
Pure accessor over the value delivered from the browser process; the renderer never computes a group id.
The literal "communications", with kDefaultDeviceId ("default") at :18. These two are the only device ids that reach JavaScript unhashed, because of the early return in GetHMACForRawMediaDeviceID.

Assembles the description list by calling four platform hooks: get_device_names, get_default_device_id, get_communications_device_id and get_group_id. The communications hook is where the platform difference enters; the input-side twin is at :313.

SOURCE OF TRUTH for the platform term. Every producer of a non-empty communications device id in the tree lives under media/audio/win/ - here and in core_audio_util_win.cc:401,469,851-852.
